newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lays new plan for return of Bosnia refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lays new plan for return of Bosnia refugees.

text.p: The United States is planning a more organised, higher-profile system for returning Bosnian refugees to their prewar homes, a senior U.S. official said on Thursday.

John Kornblum, special U.S. envoy to Bosnia, told defence writers achieving a substantial return of refugees had become the most difficult aspect of the 1995 Bosnia peace deal and threatened to undermine a central goal of the accord -- ensuring a unified Bosnia.

"What is not working -- there's no question about it, and we are quite critical of all three ethnic groups ... on this -- is people returning to homes from which they were expelled or cleansed (during the Bosnian war)," he said.

Kornblum reaffirmed that Washington would continue holding up a shipload of tanks, helicopters and guns destined for Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation until two Bosnian officials viewed as friendly to Iran were removed from office.
"Until these people have left office, the ship is going to sit there," he said.

He predicted the arms issue would be resolved but acknowledged other problems with the U.S.-led "train and equip" programme to make federation forces more nearly equal to those of the Bosnian Serbs. These included "some people taking a certain cut of the money (intended) for the training programme," he said, without giving details.

The U.S.-brokered peace accord reached at Dayton, Ohio, in 1995 guarantees refugees the right to return to their homes. But nationalist authorities across Bosnia have blocked efforts by people to move back while settling their own refugees in abandoned homes. Recently, a rising tide of ethnic violence has set the process back even more.
Kornblum said a more intense effort must be made to allow refugees to return home and prove the Dayton signatories' commitment to a unified Bosnia.

"What we need to do is set up a centralized, concerted action to identify places where resettlement is necessary but also possible; to inventory the housing stock; look at the (local) economic situation; form very frank judgments about the political-psychological situation (such as whether) there are organised groups that will try to stop (resettlement)."

Kornblum discussed such ideas with officials on a trip to Sarajevo last week and said he expected them to be a major topic of discussion in Bosnian-related meetings set for Nov. 14 in Paris and early December in London.

"It's something we're going to put a great deal of pressure and emphasis on. We're going to be working on new mechanisms to make sure (refugee return) is not just a random process but a managed process," he said.
Kornblum said he believed the internationl community would begin implementing the new programme in earnest after the winter, normally so harsh in Bosnia that activity slows.

He said he had found a "general consensus that just saying to (refugees), 'OK, here's a piece of paper that allows you to go home, here's bus fare, write and tell us how you're doing,' (will not work) and ... you need ... a systematic programme."

That means coordinating all those with influence including local Bosnian officials, police, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the International Committee of the Red Cross, economic agencies and the NATO-led implementation force (IFOR). These entities cooperate now, but informally, he said.

"We're going to have to make it a really very active focus but also high-profile programme in the spring. (I) believe very strongly the return of refugees ... to be one of the highest priorities. Otherwise some of the internal credibility of the (peace process) is going to disappear," Kornblum said.

Last week the adminstration made clear that the arms that arrived on Thursday in the Croatian port of Ploce would stay under U.S. control until Bosnia's government took several steps, including ousting Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic.

While Washington does not like Cengic's ties to Iran and Iranian forces that aided Moslems in the Bosnian war, Kornblum said the major objection was that Cengic and another official had hindered the building of joint military and other structures seen as critical to Bosnia's future.
